dietEvidence.body: No gut contents are known. The diet is not established; insectivory or omnivory are hypotheses, not observations.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: A small scansoriopterygid with an elongated third finger supporting a membranous wing. The wing membrane is preserved, but its aerodynamic function is debated.
summary: A small scansoriopterygid with an elongated third finger supporting a membranous wing. The wing membrane is preserved, but its aerodynamic function is debated.

discovery.body: Named by Xu et al., 2015. The record is known from the Tiaojishan Formation at Mutoudeng, Qinglong County, Hebei. The holotype, STM 31-2, is an articulated partial skeleton with membranous wing tissue and feathers.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: The holotype, STM 31-2, is an articulated partial skeleton with membranous wing tissue and feathers preserved on a slab and counterpart.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: The Tiaojishan Formation at Mutoudeng, Qinglong County, Hebei, records the species in the Callovian–Oxfordian. The numeric range used here is ≈165–158 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on the specimen.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The third manual digit is elongated; a rod-like styliform element extends from the wrist, and patches of membrane are preserved between the rod and digits. The tail is short. The aerodynamic function is contested.

behaviour.body: The membranous wing is preserved; whether it supported gliding, flapping or display is debated. Dececchi et al. (2020) found powered flight highly unlikely and gliding limited. Diet is inferred from anatomy; no gut contents are known.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from a single partial skeleton with membrane and feather impressions. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: V20 checked the original description’s abstract and holotype details, the open-access 2020 aerodynamic study, and the specimen record. The membrane and styliform element are direct evidence. The original authors suggested aerial locomotion; Dececchi et al. found the wing poorly suited to powered flight and limited for gliding. The functional interpretation remains contested.
